overview:
Without telling his father, Jonathan and his armourbearer cross the gorge to the Philistine garrison at Michmash, set themselves a sign, climb up on hands and feet, and kill about twenty men. Panic and an earthquake shake the Philistine camp, and Saul’s army, joined by deserters and men from hiding, routs them. But Saul has bound the troops by oath to eat nothing until evening, and Jonathan, who never heard it, tastes honey. When God gives no answer that night, the lot falls on Jonathan and Saul swears he will die; the people refuse and rescue him. A summary of Saul’s wars closes the chapter.

Two kinds of leadership run side by side. Jonathan acts on the conviction that nothing restrains the LORD from saving “by many or by few” (v. 6). Saul binds his men with oaths, calls for the priest and then cuts him off (v. 19), and in the end his own army overrules him (v. 45).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. The Talmud credits Samuel, with Gad and Nathan completing it (1 Chronicles 29:29); many scholars see it as part of a larger history compiled in the 7th–6th century BC from older sources.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it soon after the events (11th–10th century BC); many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th century BC, drawing on older court and prophetic sources.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Early in Saul’s reign, in the same campaign as chapter 13. Conventional dates put his reign about 1050–1010 BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The pass between Michmash and Geba; Saul’s camp at the edge of Gibeah; the pursuit past Beth-aven and west to Aijalon (v. 31).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: 1 Chronicles 8:33 and 9:39 list Saul’s sons as Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab and Esh-baal (compare v. 49).

hermeneutics:
Michmash is the modern village of Mukhmas, on the north side of a steep gorge known today as the Wadi es-Suweinit, with Geba facing it from the south. The chapter’s geography is exact: one rocky crag fronts Michmash on the north, the other fronts Geba on the south (vv. 4–5), and the climb takes hands as well as feet (v. 13). Isaiah 10:28–29 traces an invader’s march down the same route, leaving his baggage at Michmash and crossing “the passage” to Geba. First hearers knew the pass as a natural barrier. Two men could cross where an army could not, and a garrison on the far side had no reason to expect visitors from below.

Two verses read differently in the Septuagint, and both bear on how Saul consults God. In v. 18 the Hebrew has Saul call for “the ark of God,” though the ark had been at Kirjath-jearim for years (7:1–2). The Greek reads “the ephod,” which Ahiah is wearing in v. 3 and which held the lots used to ask God’s will. Some translators keep the Hebrew as the harder reading; others follow the Greek. In v. 41 the Hebrew is short, “Give a perfect lot.” The Greek has a full prayer, which most modern translations follow: if the guilt is in Saul or Jonathan, give Urim; if it is in the people, give Thummim (compare Exodus 28:30). That longer text shows the procedure. The lot answers yes or no, so the guilty party is found by halving: Saul and Jonathan against the people, then Saul against Jonathan (v. 42).

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence through a single long day, then closes with a summary of Saul’s reign.

rows.text: Saul’s oath and the hungry army

notes: **Saving:** the verb and its noun come 4 times. Jonathan trusts the LORD to save by many or few (v. 6); “the LORD saved Israel that day” (v. 23); Saul swears by the LORD “which saveth Israel” (v. 39); and the people credit Jonathan with “this great salvation” (v. 45).
**That day:** “day” comes 12 times. Saul’s oath runs “until evening” (v. 24), so the whole story of the honey, the slaughter and the lot plays out against the clock of one day.
**Honey and eating:** “honey” comes 5 times (vv. 25, 26, 27, 29, 43) and “eat” 8 times in vv. 24–34. The food Saul forbade is what Jonathan tasted and what the starving army fell on.

Chapter 14 is the center of chapters 13–15, Saul’s wars and rejection. It picks up from 13:23, where the Philistine garrison moves to the pass, and its closing summary (vv. 47–52) reads like the end-notice of a reign, set before the second confrontation with Samuel in chapter 15.

**Backward and forward:** the Church’s footnote at v. 20 points to Judges 7:22, where the LORD likewise set every man’s sword against his fellow in Midian’s camp. God’s silence in v. 37 returns at the end of Saul’s life, when the LORD answers him “neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets” (28:6).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote at v. 12, where Jonathan takes the Philistines’ taunt to come up as the LORD’s sign, points to a Nephite commander who reasoned the other way. When his people asked to go up into the mountains against the Gadianton robbers, Gidgiddoni answered that if they went up “the Lord would deliver us into their hands,” and he waited for the enemy to come down. The two passages set the same question side by side: when to attack and when to wait, and how to know which the Lord wants.

traditions.date: LDS edition of the King James Bible, 1979
traditions.text: The footnote at v. 45, where the people refuse to let Saul kill Jonathan, points to the Topical Guide entry on common consent. That entry lists the verse with the instruction to the Church that “all things shall be done by common consent” (D&C 26:2). The people’s voice overrules a king’s oath here, and the footnote reads that as an early example of the principle.

In Josephus, Saul has the high priest put on his vestments and prophesy, and is promised victory. Josephus then calls Saul’s curse an act “liable to be very much blamed,” made either in ignorance or in the giddiness of an unexpected victory. His curse forbids anyone to stop the slaughter to eat before night, and Jonathan, on hearing of it, says his father had not done well, since fed men would have killed more.

When the lot falls on Jonathan, Josephus gives him a speech of his own. He asks his father not to spare him: death will be welcome coming from his father’s piety after so great a victory, and it is consolation enough to leave the Hebrews victorious. The people are grieved and swear they will not see the author of their victory die, and so they snatch him from his father. Josephus turns Jonathan into a model of filial piety ready to die for an oath he never heard.

The Aramaic translation adds a reason to the people’s defense of Jonathan in v. 45: “it is revealed before the Lord” that he acted in error that day. He had not heard the oath, so in the Targum’s eyes he never broke it knowingly. In v. 41 it turns Saul’s terse plea into a request that God bring the matter out in truth. Both changes protect Jonathan’s name: the lot finds him, but the Targum makes clear that heaven knew he meant no wrong.

The rabbis use v. 24 in a legal question: does the word “cursed” carry the force of an oath? The verse says Saul adjured the people with a curse on any man who ate, and v. 27 calls the same words an oath, so a curse can bind like one. Elsewhere they treat Jonathan’s honey as medicine: someone seized with faintness from hunger should be fed honey and sweets, which restore the eyes, and the hint is Jonathan’s “mine eyes have been enlightened” (v. 29).

The great stone Saul has rolled up (v. 33) becomes, in the rabbis’ reading, a private altar for slaughter, and they note that the people slaughtered there by day and then at night (v. 34), which helps them decide what could be done at such altars. Rav Hisda takes Saul’s “slay them here” to mean that Saul checked the knife himself, the source for inspecting a slaughtering knife.

Rashi reads the honey in the wood as sugar cane, which he says grew in the land of Israel, flowing from the canes, and he cites Rabbi Nathan that sugar is called *sukkar* in Arabic. For “ark of God” in v. 18 he explains that Saul meant the Urim and Thummim, so the priest could ask God. On v. 32 he offers his own view that the people killed a mother and its young on the same day, against Leviticus 22:28, and reports the rabbis’ view that they had made the animals peace offerings and ate before the blood was sprinkled.

Against Marcion’s claim that the Creator is harsh, Tertullian lists his acts of mercy, among them the mercy that spared Saul’s son, about to die, at the people’s plea. In a later book he says Jonathan “blotted out by his deprecation” the guilt of breaking the fast. Tertullian treats Jonathan as guilty and forgiven, where the Targum treats him as innocent through ignorance.
